course.name: Mathematical Methods for the Physical Sciences II

question.text:
Let $F(x) = \sin(2x)$ for $x\in\mathbb R.$ Suppose $f(x)$ is the $\pi$-periodic extension of $F(x)$ from $x \in [0,\pi)$ to $x \in \mathbb{R}.$ Which of the following statements are true?

  1. $f(x+\pi) = f(x)$ for all $x \in \mathbb{R}$
  2. $f(x) = F(x)$ for all $x \in \mathbb{R}$
  3. $f\left(x+\dfrac{5\pi}{2}\right) = f(x)$ for all $x \in \mathbb{R}$
question.explanation:
Since $f$ is the $\pi$-periodic extension of $F,$ we have

  • $f(x+\pi)=f(x)$ for all $x\in\mathbb{R},$ and

  • $f(x)=F(x)$ for all $x \in [0,\pi).$

With that in mind, let's examine our statements in turn.

  • Statement I is true. This is exactly the definition of $\pi$-periodicity: \[ f(x+\pi)=f(x) \] for all $x\in\mathbb{R}.$

  • Statement II is true. Notice that $F$ itself is $\pi$-periodic, because for any $x\in\mathbb{R},$ we have \begin{align*} F(x+\pi) = \sin(2(x+\pi)) = \sin(2x+2\pi) = \sin(2x) = F(x). \end{align*} Since $F$ already satisfies the periodicity rule, the $\pi$-periodic extension agrees with $F$ everywhere, so $f(x)=F(x)$ for all $x\in\mathbb{R}.$

  • Statement III is false. Since $f$ is $\pi$-periodic, shifting by $2\pi$ does not change the value of $f,$ so \begin{align*} f\left(x+\dfrac{5\pi}{2}\right) = f\left(\left(x+\dfrac{\pi}{2}\right)+2\pi\right) = f\left(x+\dfrac{\pi}{2}\right). \end{align*} But $f\left(x+\dfrac{\pi}{2}\right)$ does not always equal $f(x).$ For example, take $x=\dfrac{\pi}{3}.$ Then, \begin{align*} f\left(\dfrac{\pi}{3}+\dfrac{\pi}{2}\right) = f\left(\dfrac{5\pi}{6}\right) = F\left(\dfrac{5\pi}{6}\right) = \sin\left(\dfrac{5\pi}{6}\right) = \dfrac{1}{2}, \end{align*} while \begin{align*} f\left(\dfrac{\pi}{3}\right) = F\left(\dfrac{\pi}{3}\right) = \sin\left(\dfrac{\pi}{3}\right)=\dfrac{\sqrt 3}{2}. \end{align*} Hence, $f\left(x+\dfrac{5\pi}{2}\right) \neq f(x)$ for $x=\dfrac{\pi}{4}.$

Therefore, the correct answer is "I and II only".

example.title: Understanding the Periodic Extension of a Function

question.text:
\[ \langle f(x),g(x) \rangle = \displaystyle\int_{-\pi}^{\pi} f(x) g(x) \, \textrm{d}x \]

Given the inner product on the set of continuous functions over $x\in [-\pi,\pi)$ defined above, select the correct options below.
question.explanation:
We begin by using the product-to-sum identity \[ \cos(3x)\cos(6x)=\dfrac{1}{2}\big(\cos(3x)+\cos(9x)\big). \]

Substituting this into the integral gives \begin{align*} \langle \cos(3x), \cos(6x) \rangle &= \int_{-\pi}^{\pi} \cos(3x)\cos(6x)\,\text{d}x \\[5pt] &= \int_{-\pi}^{\pi} \dfrac{1}{2}\cos(3x)+\dfrac{1}{2}\cos(9x)\:\text{d}x \\[5pt] &= \left[ \dfrac{1}{6} \sin(3x)+\dfrac{1}{18}\sin(9x)\right]_{-\pi}^{\pi} \\[5pt] &= \dfrac{1}{6}\big(\sin(3\pi)-\sin(-3\pi)\big)+\dfrac{1}{18}\big(\sin(9\pi)-\sin(-9\pi)\big) \\[5pt] &= \dfrac{1}{6}(0-0)+\dfrac{1}{18}(0-0) \\[5pt] &= \bbox[4pt, border: solid 1pt gainsboro]{0}. \end{align*}

Therefore, $f(x)=\cos(3x)$ and $g(x)=\cos(6x)$ $\bbox[4pt, border: solid 1pt gainsboro]{\text{are orthogonal}}$ with respect to the inner product.

example.title: Checking Orthogonality of Sines and Cosines

question.text:
Let $F(x) = x^2+3$ for $x\in\mathbb R,$ and let $f(x)$ be the $2\pi$-periodic extension of $F$ from $x\in [-\pi,\pi)$ to $x\in \mathbb R.$ The Fourier series of $f$ is given by

\[ f(x) \sim \dfrac{a_0}{2} + \sum_{n=1}^\infty \left(a_n \cos(nx) + b_n \sin(nx)\right). \] Select the correct options in the expression for the coefficient $a_3$ below, where $\langle \:,\rangle$ denotes the usual inner product on functions over $[-\pi,\pi).$
question.explanation:
The usual inner product of functions $f$ and $g$ over $x\in [-\pi,\pi)$ is given by \[ \langle f(x),g(x) \rangle = \int_{-\pi}^{\pi} f(x)g(x)\,\textrm{d}x. \]

For a $2\pi$-periodic function $f(x)$ that is piecewise continuous over $x\in [-\pi,\pi),$ the Fourier series of $f$ is given by \[ f(x) \sim \dfrac{a_0}{2}+\sum_{n=1}^{\infty}\left( a_n\cos(nx)+b_n\sin(nx)\right), \] where $a_0,$ $a_n,$ and $b_n$ are constants to be determined.

Now, we find the inner product of $f(x)$ with $\cos(3x){:}$

\begin{align*} \left\langle f(x), \cos(3x) \right\rangle &=\\[5pt] \left\langle \dfrac{a_0}{2}+\sum_{n=1}^{\infty} \left(a_n\cos(nx)+b_n\sin(nx)\right), \cos(3x) \right\rangle &=\\[5pt] \left\langle \dfrac{a_0}{2},\cos(3x) \right\rangle + \sum_{n=1}^{\infty} \left\langle a_n\cos(nx), \cos(3x) \right\rangle + \sum_{n=1}^{\infty} \left\langle b_n\sin(nx), \cos(3x) \right\rangle &=\\[5pt] \dfrac{a_0}{2} \left\langle 1,\cos(3x) \right\rangle + \sum_{n=1}^{\infty} a_n \left\langle \cos(nx), \cos(3x) \right\rangle + \sum_{n=1}^{\infty}b_n \left\langle \sin(nx), \cos(3x) \right\rangle \end{align*}

Since the functions $ 1, \sin(x), \cos(x), \sin(2x), \cos(2x), \ldots $ are orthogonal with respect to the defined inner product, the only nonzero term in the final expression above is \[ a_3 \left\langle \cos(3x), \cos(3x) \right\rangle. \]

Computing the inner product, we have \begin{align*} \left\langle \cos(3x), \cos(3x) \right\rangle &= \int_{-\pi}^{\pi} \cos^2(3x)\,\textrm{d}x \\[5pt] &= \int_{-\pi}^{\pi} \dfrac{1}{2}+\dfrac{1}{2}\cos(6x) \:\textrm{d}x \\[5pt] &= \left[ \dfrac{1}{2} x + \dfrac{1}{12} \sin(6x) \right]_{-\pi}^{\pi} \\[5pt] &= \dfrac{1}{2} (\pi - (-\pi)) + \dfrac{1}{12} (\sin(6\pi) - \sin(-6\pi)) \\[5pt] &= \pi. \end{align*}

Finally, we obtain that \begin{align*} \left\langle f(x), \cos(3x) \right\rangle &= a_3 \left\langle \cos(3x), \cos(3x) \right\rangle \\[5pt] a_3 &= \bbox[4pt, border: solid 1pt gainsboro]{\dfrac{\left\langle f(x), \cos(3x) \right\rangle}{\left\langle \cos(3x), \cos(3x) \right\rangle} }\\[5pt] a_3 &= \dfrac{1}{\pi} \int_{-\pi}^{\pi} f(x)\cos(3x)\,\textrm{d}x \\[5pt] &= \bbox[4pt, border: solid 1pt gainsboro]{\dfrac{1}{\pi} } \cdot \bbox[4pt, border: solid 1pt gainsboro]{\int_{-\pi}^{\pi} (x^2+3)\cos(3x)\,\textrm{d}x}. \end{align*}

question.text: \[ \langle f(x),g(x) \rangle = \displaystyle\int_{-\pi}^{\pi} f(x) g(x) \, \textrm{d}x \] Given the inner product on the set of continuous functions over $x\in [-\pi,\pi]$ defined above, select the correct options below.
question.explanation:
Evaluating the inner product, we obtain \begin{align*} \langle \sin(6x), 1 \rangle &= \int_{-\pi}^{\pi} \sin(6x)\,\text{d}x \\[5pt] &= \left[ -\dfrac{1}{6}\cos(6x) \right]_{-\pi}^{\pi} \\[5pt] &= -\dfrac{1}{6}\big(\cos(6\pi)-\cos(-6\pi)\big) \\[5pt] &= -\dfrac{1}{6}(1-1) \\[5pt] &= \bbox[4pt, border: solid 1pt gainsboro]{0}. \end{align*}

Therefore, $f(x)=\sin(6x)$ and $g(x)=1$ $\bbox[4pt, border: solid 1pt gainsboro]{\text{are orthogonal}}$ with respect to the inner product.

example.title: Checking Orthogonality of Sines and Cosines

question.text:
Let $F(x) = x^2-2x+1$ for $x\in\mathbb R,$ and let $f(x)$ be the $2\pi$-periodic extension of $F$ from $x\in [0,2\pi)$ to $x\in \mathbb R.$ The Fourier series of $f$ is given by

\[ f(x) \sim \dfrac{a_0}{2} + \sum_{n=1}^\infty \left(a_n \cos(nx) + b_n \sin(nx)\right). \] Select the correct options in the expression for the coefficient $a_4$ below, where $\langle \:,\rangle$ denotes the usual inner product on functions over $[0,2\pi).$
question.explanation:
The usual inner product of functions $f$ and $g$ over $x\in [0,2\pi)$ is given by \[ \langle f(x),g(x) \rangle = \int_{0}^{2\pi} f(x)g(x)\,\textrm{d}x. \]

For a $2\pi$-periodic function $f(x)$ that is piecewise continuous over $x\in [0,2\pi),$ the Fourier series of $f$ is given by \[ f(x) \sim \dfrac{a_0}{2}+\sum_{n=1}^{\infty}\left( a_n\cos(nx)+b_n\sin(nx)\right), \] where $a_0,$ $a_n,$ and $b_n$ are constants to be determined.

Now, we find the inner product of $f(x)$ with $\cos(4x){:}$

\begin{align*} \left\langle f(x), \cos(4x) \right\rangle &=\\[5pt] \left\langle \dfrac{a_0}{2}+\sum_{n=1}^{\infty} \left(a_n\cos(nx)+b_n\sin(nx)\right), \cos(4x) \right\rangle &=\\[5pt] \left\langle \dfrac{a_0}{2},\cos(4x) \right\rangle + \sum_{n=1}^{\infty} \left\langle a_n\cos(nx), \cos(4x) \right\rangle + \sum_{n=1}^{\infty} \left\langle b_n\sin(nx), \cos(4x) \right\rangle &=\\[5pt] \dfrac{a_0}{2} \left\langle 1,\cos(4x) \right\rangle + \sum_{n=1}^{\infty} a_n \left\langle \cos(nx), \cos(4x) \right\rangle + \sum_{n=1}^{\infty}b_n \left\langle \sin(nx), \cos(4x) \right\rangle \end{align*}

Since the functions $ 1, \sin(x), \cos(x), \sin(2x), \cos(2x), \ldots $ are orthogonal with respect to the defined inner product, the only nonzero term in the final expression above is \[ a_4 \left\langle \cos(4x), \cos(4x) \right\rangle. \]

Computing the inner product, we have \begin{align*} \left\langle \cos(4x), \cos(4x) \right\rangle &= \int_{0}^{2\pi} \cos^2(4x)\,\textrm{d}x \\[5pt] &= \int_{0}^{2\pi} \dfrac{1}{2}+\dfrac{1}{2}\cos(8x) \:\textrm{d}x \\[5pt] &= \left[ \dfrac{1}{2} x + \dfrac{1}{16} \sin(8x) \right]_{0}^{2\pi} \\[5pt] &= \dfrac{1}{2} (2\pi - 0) - \dfrac{1}{16} (\sin(16\pi) - \sin(0)) \\[5pt] &= \pi. \end{align*}

Finally, we obtain that \begin{align*} \left\langle f(x), \cos(4x) \right\rangle &= a_4 \left\langle \cos(4x), \cos(4x) \right\rangle \\[5pt] a_4 &= \bbox[4pt, border: solid 1pt gainsboro]{\dfrac{\left\langle f(x), \cos(4x) \right\rangle}{\left\langle \cos(4x), \cos(4x) \right\rangle} }\\[5pt] a_4 &= \dfrac{1}{\pi} \int_{0}^{2\pi} f(x)\cos(4x)\,\textrm{d}x \\[5pt] &= \bbox[4pt, border: solid 1pt gainsboro]{\dfrac{1}{\pi} } \cdot \bbox[4pt, border: solid 1pt gainsboro]{\int_{0}^{2\pi} (x^2-2x+1)\cos(4x)\,\textrm{d}x}. \end{align*}
